title: Bringing his first charts to Buddy Rich and the RCA recording
summary: On unemployment he took a bus to Philadelphia with pencil parts for Rich, and the RCA Victor recording followed; Rich cut sections by instinct.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: it to your apartment, because you know it’s not worth anything, it’s just like a used car, they’ll give you so much for the trade in. Anyway, long story short, I was on unemployment and I heard that Buddy had signed, Pat told me that Buddy had signed with RCA Victor. And so I was making fifty bucks a week on unemployment and then doing odd jobs. A bus trip to Philadelphia was 25 bucks. So I bought a bus ticket to Philadelphia with this “Piece of the Road” suite that I wrote. And everybody was there at the club, Brandy’s Wharf in Philadelphia. You know Don Sebesky, all the guys were there with charts. So it was a cattle call. So I was there, put on the chart down, I’ve actually got a cassette of the rehearsal, and you know Buddy didn’t play he just sat there. And there was a, they started with a ballad which was unusual for Jimmy Mosher, and then there was a rock piece, and then a solo piano and then a jazz waltz. When we got to the jazz waltz part, after about, I don’t know maybe about half the chart, maybe not even half the chart, he stopped. And he went and sat down at the drums and played it. And at the end he says, “Okay, I want you in New York in a couple of weeks and we’re going to record your stuff.” Just like that. And you know I said, “Yeah, sure, right.” You know. But that was it. He said, “You’re in.” And you know I’ve told this story before but that really put me on the map, writing for Buddy Rich. I mean you can’t get any bigger than that.
Man, I bet your made sure that the parts were all correct. I mean did you do the copying by yourself at that time?

You would think I would do that. You would think I would make all kinds of painful reviewing. But luckily a lot of the guys in the band were my friends and they corrected a lot of mistakes for me. The parts were in pencil. The parts were in pencil. However, when we finally got to the RCA Victor recording, this was in the old days when the record companies paid for the copyist, they paid the composer and the arranger, everything was union scale. So I was on the road with a man named Milt Newman who had worked as a copyist. He taught me how to copy. But then I befriended a good colleague of his, Larry Abel, who became my copyist for years. And he did all the copying and it was all done you know, the right way, and the record company paid for it. The copyist got residuals.
Wow. What did you expect from him? Did you trust him to come to you and say, “Listen John, measure 46 you’ve got this note that, I don’t think it’s what you want. Would he do that?
No he would just say something’s wrong there. Or I don’t like that section cut it out. And you’d have to do it. It’s like Mancini said, it’s like giving up one of your children but you
have to do it, you can’t fall in love with every note you write. Because he knows more than you do about what he’s presenting.
